title: Backlighting the Cosmic Web with Fast Radio Bursts: An Anthology of Dispersion Measure Cross-Correlations with Large-Scale Structure and Baryon Tracers
summary: Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) probe baryons permeating the cosmic web through their dispersion measures (DMs), which encode the integrated electron density along cosmological sightlines. Using 3,455 unique FRB sources from CHIME/FRB with $\sim 15$ arcmin localizations, we present an anthology of DM correlations with tracers of large-scale structure and baryonic matter at redshifts $z \lesssim 1.5$. We measure statistically significant correlations at $2.6-5σ$ with ten probes, including galaxies ($2.8σ$), weak gravitational lensing ($2.6σ$), cosmic infrared background ($4.0σ$), cosmic microwave background (CMB) lensing ($3.3σ$), thermal Sunyaev Zel'dovich (tSZ) effect ($3.8σ$), X-ray emission tracing galaxy clusters ($5.0σ$) and superclusters ($3.3σ$), soft X-ray background (SXRB, $4.1σ$), and radio continuum emission ($3.2σ$). These measurements reveal a consistent picture in which FRB sightlines intersecting overdense environments carry systematically larger DMs. Correlations with hot-gas tracers provide additional leverage on the strength of feedback, as they are strongly weighted towards the dense, bound gas. The measured amplitude of tSZ$\times$DM and SXRB$\times$DM correlations are consistent with theoretical predictions of baryon distribution from a DM-$z$ relation-inferred model with moderate feedback at $\sim 0.5σ$ level. Weaker feedback scenario is ruled out at $\sim 3.5σ$ by the SXRB$\times$DM correlation. Taken together, these measurements constitute a quantitative multi-tracer foundation for a new era in which FRBs from next generation facilities, such as BURSTT, CHORD, DSA, and SKA, in harmony with other probes, will map the baryon content of the full extent of the cosmic web.

AI.tldr: Using 3,455 CHIME/FRB sources, this study finds strong correlations between FRB dispersion measures and multiple large-scale baryonic tracers, confirming that FRBs trace overdense cosmic environments and providing empirical support for baryon distribution models with moderate feedback. This paves the way for future FRB observations to map the cosmic web's baryon content.
AI.motivation: The study aims to use Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) as probes to investigate the distribution of baryons in the cosmic web by analyzing their dispersion measures (DMs) along cosmological sightlines.
AI.method: The authors utilize 3,455 unique FRB sources from CHIME/FRB with high-precision localizations (~15 arcmin) to measure correlations between FRB dispersion measures and multiple tracers of large-scale structure and baryonic matter at redshifts z ≤ 1.5. They perform statistical correlation analyses with ten different probes including galaxies, weak gravitational lensing, cosmic backgrounds, and various X-ray and radio observations.
AI.result: They detect statistically significant correlations (2.6–5σ) between FRB DMs and ten tracers of baryonic matter and large-scale structure, revealing that FRB sightlines intersecting overdense environments yield systematically larger DMs. The observed amplitude of thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ) and soft X-ray background (SXRB) correlations with DM align with theoretical baryon distribution models that include moderate feedback. The data disfavors weaker feedback models at ~3.5σ significance. This multi-tracer correlation study quantitatively supports the use of FRBs in mapping cosmic baryon distribution.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a robust observational foundation demonstrating that FRBs are effective probes of baryon distribution in the cosmic web. Correlations of FRB DMs with various large-scale structure tracers validate theoretical models and will enable future FRB surveys to comprehensively map baryonic matter across cosmological scales.

title: Caustic Skeleton and the Local Cosmic Web: the Coma Cluster node and the Pisces-Perseus ridge
summary: We apply caustic skeleton theory to the Manticore-Local simulations, which are Bayesian constrained reconstructions of the Local Universe from the 2M++ galaxy catalogue, and extract the three-dimensional multi-scale caustic skeleton of two canonical weblike structures in our Local Universe, namely the Coma Cluster and the Pisces-Perseus ridge as they represent the most prominent cluster node and filamentary artery in the nearby Universe. We show that the Caustic Skeleton network of caustic singularities accurately reproduces the observed large-scale organisation of galaxies in redshift space for one of the Manticore realisations. The hierarchy of caustic features allows us to establish a multi-scale classification of the large-scale environment in which observed 2M++ galaxies reside. One of the most interesting aspects of the theory is that it predicts two topologically distinct classes of filaments (A_4 swallowtail and D_4 umbilic caustics) that form through fundamentally different folding histories yet appear morphologically similar enough, on the surface, to be overlooked by conventional structure identifiers. We find that the influence of D_4 filaments only becomes increasingly relevant towards smaller scales, and the Pisces-Perseus Supercluster in particular is revealed to be a distinctly D_4-dominated structure compared to the extended Stickman structure around the Coma Cluster. In other words, caustic skeleton theory enables a novel topological characterisation of one of the most studied filamentary complexes in the nearby Universe. [Shortened]

AI.tldr: This paper uses caustic skeleton theory on Bayesian simulations of the Local Universe to uncover and classify distinct topological filament types and multi-scale structures, enhancing our understanding of cosmic web morphology around important clusters like Coma and Pisces-Perseus.
AI.motivation: To understand and classify the large-scale structure of the Local Universe by applying caustic skeleton theory to Bayesian constrained simulations, enabling the identification of distinct topological classes of filaments and improving the characterization of cosmic web structures.
AI.method: Applying caustic skeleton theory to Manticore-Local simulations derived from the 2M++ galaxy catalogue, extracting three-dimensional multi-scale caustic skeletons for the Coma Cluster and Pisces-Perseus ridge, and analyzing the hierarchy of caustic features to classify large-scale environments.
AI.result: The Caustic Skeleton network accurately reproduces observed galaxy organization in redshift space, reveals two distinct topological filament classes (A_4 swallowtail and D_4 umbilic caustics), with D_4 filaments dominating smaller scale structures such as the Pisces-Perseus Supercluster, providing a novel topological characterization of filamentary complexes.
AI.conclusion: Caustic skeleton theory effectively reveals the multi-scale, topologically distinct nature of cosmic filaments in the Local Universe, offering a new framework for classifying and understanding filamentary and cluster structures beyond traditional morphological methods.

title: Testing $Λ$CDM with ANN-Reconstructed Expansion History from Cosmic Chronometers
summary: In modern cosmology, the rapid growth of high-precision observational data, along with significant theoretical advances, has intensified the challenge of identifying a robust, model-independent framework to probe the expansion history of the Universe. In this work, we propose a novel artificial neural network (ANN)-based framework for the non-parametric reconstruction of the late-time cosmic expansion. The framework is trained and validated through a three-stage screening pipeline prior to its application to real observational data. As a demonstration of its effectiveness, we reconstruct the Hubble parameter $H(z)$ using the latest cosmic chronometer measurements. Our results show that the reconstructed expansion history aligns with the predictions of the $Λ$CDM model within observational uncertainties, thereby supporting the robustness and reliability of the proposed approach.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an ANN-based framework for reconstructing the late-time cosmic expansion non-parametrically, validating it through a rigorous pipeline, and successfully applying it to cosmic chronometer data, yielding results consistent with the $Λ$CDM model.
AI.motivation: The challenge of identifying a robust, model-independent framework to probe the Universe's expansion history due to increasing high-precision observational data and theoretical advances.
AI.method: Development of a novel artificial neural network (ANN)-based framework for non-parametric reconstruction of late-time cosmic expansion, trained and validated through a three-stage screening pipeline.
AI.result: Reconstruction of the Hubble parameter $H(z)$ from the latest cosmic chronometer measurements aligns with the $Λ$CDM model predictions within observational uncertainties, demonstrating the framework's robustness and reliability.
AI.conclusion: The ANN-based, non-parametric reconstruction framework provides a reliable, model-independent tool for probing the late-time cosmic expansion consistent with existing cosmological models.

title: Constraints on the Primordial Black Hole Abundance using Pulsar Parameter Drifts
summary: Primordial black holes (PBHs) provide a compelling interpretation for the binary black holes (BBHs) observed by ground-based gravitational-wave (GW) detectors, especially for those BBHs in the theoretical mass gap. In the early Universe, the scalar perturbations required to produce such PBHs inevitably generate scalar-induced GWs (SIGWs). These SIGWs peak in the sub-nanohertz band, and manifest secularly as measurable jerk-like drifts in the second derivative of pulsar spin periods. In this Letter, we perform the first search for SIGWs using pulsar parameter drifts, and place a 95\% confidence-level upper limit on the PBH abundance of $f_{\mathrm{PBH}} < 10^{-10}$ over the mass range $[3 \times 10^{-1}, 4 \times 10^{4}] M_{\odot}$. Our results strongly disfavor a PBH origin for the BBHs currently detected by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK) Collaborations.

AI.tldr: This study uses pulsar timing to set strong upper limits on primordial black hole abundance, ruling out PBHs as the main origin of binary black holes observed by gravitational-wave detectors.
AI.motivation: To test the primordial black hole (PBH) hypothesis for the origin of observed binary black holes (BBHs), particularly those in the theoretical mass gap, by searching for associated scalar-induced gravitational waves (SIGWs).
AI.method: Performing the first search for SIGWs using secular jerk-like drifts in the second derivative of pulsar spin periods caused by SIGWs in the sub-nanohertz band.
AI.result: Established a 95% confidence-level upper limit on PBH abundance of f_PBH < 10^-10 across the mass range [0.3, 4 × 10^4] solar masses, strongly disfavoring the PBH explanation for BBHs detected by LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA.
AI.conclusion: The stringent upper limit on PBH abundance derived from pulsar timing data excludes PBHs as a significant source of the observed BBHs in current gravitational-wave detections, challenging the PBH hypothesis for these events.

title: Reionization, UV Luminosity and 21$\,$cm Sensitivity to Primordial Magnetic Fields: Impact of Energy Losses
summary: Magnetic fields with field strengths between $10^{-17}\,$G and a few Nanogauss are expected to exist today in the intergalactic medium (IGM). Their origin is unknown, but may be of primordial nature, in which case they would have influenced the thermal and ionization history of the IGM as well as the growth of small-scale matter perturbations. In this work, we revisit constraints on Primordial Magnetic fields (PMFs) by consistently accounting for their energy losses through ambipolar diffusion and decaying turbulences from recombination through the epoch of reionization, which progressively reduces the magnetic field strength over time. We implement these effects in ${\tt HyRec}$ and ${\tt exo21cmFAST}$ to model the interplay between PMFs and astrophysical processes up to reionization. Using a neural-network emulator (${\tt NNERO}$), we perform a MCMC analysis that combines late-time probes of the reionization history and galaxy UV luminosity functions. We find that including PMF energy losses significantly relaxes previous bounds, as the reduced field strength suppresses their imprint on observables. Employing a Fisher matrix analysis, we estimate the sensitivity of the 21$\,$cm signal experiment HERA to the PMFs' imprint on intergalactic medium perturbations and show that 21$\,$cm cosmology could significantly improve on current bounds. Our results highlight the importance of modeling PMF evolution self-consistently with the IGM evolution to extract current bounds and future sensitivities.

AI.tldr: This paper revisits constraints on primordial magnetic fields by incorporating their energy losses during cosmic evolution, uses advanced simulations combined with neural network-based MCMC to analyze data, and finds that accounting for these losses relaxes previous bounds. It also demonstrates that future 21 cm cosmology experiments, like HERA, could greatly improve constraints on PMFs.
AI.motivation: To understand and constrain the origin and evolution of primordial magnetic fields (PMFs) and their impact on the intergalactic medium (IGM) and cosmic history.
AI.method: The work models PMF energy losses through ambipolar diffusion and decaying turbulences from recombination to reionization, integrating these effects into ${\tt HyRec}$ and ${\tt exo21cmFAST}$. A neural-network emulator (${\tt NNERO}$) is used to perform MCMC analysis combining reionization history and galaxy UV luminosity data. Fisher matrix analysis is applied to estimate 21 cm experiment (HERA) sensitivity.
AI.result: Accounting for PMF energy losses relaxes previous constraints on PMFs by reducing their observable imprint. The study shows that 21 cm cosmology experiments could substantially improve current bounds. Self-consistent PMF and IGM evolution modeling is critical for accurate constraints and sensitivity predictions.
AI.conclusion: Including PMF energy losses in modeling is essential to correctly constrain primordial magnetic fields. Future 21 cm experiments hold promise for significantly advancing constraints on PMFs' effects in the IGM.

title: Electromagnetic Precursors to Binary Neutron Star Mergers: Kinetic Simulations of Magnetospheric Flaring
summary: We present the first 3D global kinetic simulations of the interacting magnetospheres of pre-merger binary neutron stars. The stars, whose magnetic moments are anti-aligned, twist the field lines connecting them, leading to periodic eruptions. Each eruption consists of an expanding magnetic flux tube with a reconnecting current sheet trailing behind it, topologically analogous to coronal mass ejections. We predict two novel classes of electromagnetic precursor signals powered by the efficient dissipation of magnetic energy in these periodically forming trailing current sheets. First, particles accelerated in the sheets produce nonthermal gamma-ray signals peaking at $\sim16\,\mathrm{MeV}$, which escape minutes to seconds before merger while the sheets are still optically thin to pair production, with modest characteristic luminosities of $L_\mathrm{obs}\gtrsim 10^{42}\,\mathrm{erg/s}$, detectable only for nearby mergers. Second, merging plasmoids in the sheets could produce fast radio burst-like transients in the final seconds before merger, with characteristic luminosities $L_\mathrm{radio}\sim 10^{38-40}\,\mathrm{erg/s}$. These coherent radio precursors would be detectable by upcoming instruments, either in untargeted surveys by wide-field instruments such as CHORD, or through targeted follow-up of gravitational-wave early-warning alerts with instruments such as DSA or SKA-mid.

AI.tldr: This paper uses 3D global kinetic simulations to show that interacting magnetospheres of pre-merger binary neutron stars produce periodic magnetic eruptions leading to gamma-ray and fast radio burst-like precursors detectable shortly before merger.
AI.motivation: To understand the electromagnetic precursor signals arising from the interaction of magnetospheres in pre-merger binary neutron stars, which can inform observational strategies preceding neutron star mergers.
AI.method: Conducting the first 3D global kinetic simulations of the interacting magnetospheres of pre-merger binary neutron stars with anti-aligned magnetic moments, focusing on the dynamics of twisted field lines and resulting eruptions.
AI.result: Identification of periodic eruptions consisting of expanding magnetic flux tubes with trailing reconnecting current sheets; prediction of two classes of electromagnetic precursor signals: nonthermal gamma-ray emission peaking at ~16 MeV detectable seconds to minutes before merger, and fast radio burst-like transients from merging plasmoids seconds before merger.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that binary neutron star magnetospheric interactions produce distinct electromagnetic precursor signals that can be detected by current and upcoming gamma-ray and radio instruments, enhancing early-warning capabilities for mergers.

title: Precision Analysis for $\boldsymbol{H_0}$ Using Upcoming Multi-band Gravitational Wave Observations
summary: We investigate how multi-band gravitational wave (GW) observations can constrain the uncertainties in the Hubble parameter ($H_0$) using primordial black holes (PBHs) as possible sources. Our framework combines scalar-induced and merger-induced GWs from PBHs, and forecasts on a combination of two future detectors Square Kilometre Array (SKA) and the Einstein Telescope (ET), enabling a multi-band analysis. We perform a statistical forecast of the PBH parameters, $M_{\rm PBH}$ and $f_{\rm PBH}$, using signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) estimates and Fisher matrix analysis. Imposing $\mathrm{SNR} \geq 1$, we identify the accessible PBH parameter space and propagate these uncertainties to estimate the corresponding uncertainties in $H_0$. For $δθ_i/θ_i \leq 0.1$, with $θ_i \equiv M_{\rm PBH}(f_{\rm PBH})$, we find $δH_0 \lesssim 2~{\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ in a conservative approach, improving to $δH_0 \lesssim \mathcal{O}(0.1)~{\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ for $δθ_i/θ_i \leq 0.01$ for an optimistic approach of precision measurement. The results are further found to be largely insensitive to the fiducial choice of the $H_0$, with only moderate dependence on the PBH collapse efficiency. These findings demonstrate that multi-band GW observations provide an independent and complementary approach to constraining the uncertainties in $H_0$, with the potential to provide a novel, cosmic distance ladder-independent measure of the Hubble parameter.

AI.tldr: This study uses multi-band gravitational wave observations from primordial black holes with SKA and ET detectors to forecast constraints on $H_0$. With statistical methods, uncertainties in PBH parameters were propagated to estimate $H_0$'s uncertainty, achieving precision down to $\sim0.1\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ under optimistic scenarios, independent of traditional cosmic distance ladders.
AI.motivation: To investigate how multi-band gravitational wave observations using primordial black holes as sources can constrain uncertainties in the Hubble parameter $H_0$.
AI.method: Combined scalar-induced and merger-induced gravitational wave signals from primordial black holes were analyzed using a forecast framework involving two future detectors (SKA and ET) to perform multi-band analysis. A statistical forecast of PBH parameters ($M_{PBH}$ and $f_{PBH}$) was conducted using signal-to-noise ratio estimates and Fisher matrix analysis.
AI.result: Accessible PBH parameter space was identified with SNR $\geq 1$, uncertainties in PBH parameters were propagated to obtain uncertainties in $H_0$. Conservative estimates yield $\delta H_0  \lesssim 2\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ for relative PBH parameter uncertainties of 0.1, improving to $\delta H_0 \lesssim \mathcal{O}(0.1)\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ for 0.01 relative uncertainties with optimistic precision. The results are largely insensitive to fiducial $H_0$ and moderately dependent on PBH collapse efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Multi-band gravitational wave observations provide an independent, complementary, and potentially precise method to constrain $H_0$ uncertainties, offering a cosmic distance ladder-independent measurement of the Hubble parameter.

title: Downward ultra-high-energy neutrino detection in the air with radio antennas at ground-based observatories
summary: Ultra-high-energy (UHE) neutrinos are unique cosmic messengers that can traverse cosmological distances unattenuated, providing direct insight into the most energetic processes in the universe. Radio detection offers significant advantages for detecting highly inclined air showers induced by UHE neutrinos. This is due to a larger exposure range compared to particle detectors, which is a result of minimal atmospheric attenuation of radio signals combined with good reconstruction precision. Furthermore, this technique improves the air shower longitudinal reconstruction, which can be used to identify neutrinos with their first interaction far below the top of the atmosphere. In this work, we present a method for identifying UHE neutrinos using ground-based radio antennas. A reconstruction algorithm is introduced based on the radio emission maximum ($X^{\text{radio}}_{\text{max}}$), which demonstrates its power in distinguishing deeply developing neutrino-induced showers from background cosmic rays. Using simulations of $ν_e$-CC-induced air showers, we evaluate the trigger efficiency, reconstruction performance, and resulting effective area and aperture prediction for a reference array. Our results show that radio detection significantly enhances the sensitivity to very inclined showers above 1 EeV, complementing traditional surface detectors. This technique is highly scalable and applicable to future radio observatories, such as GRAND. The proposed reconstruction and identification strategy provides a pathway toward achieving the sensitivity required to detect UHE neutrinos.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a radio detection method with a reconstruction algorithm based on maximum radio emission depth to identify ultra-high-energy neutrinos in inclined air showers, significantly improving sensitivity and complementing existing detectors, with applications to future observatories such as GRAND.
AI.motivation: UHE neutrinos are unique cosmic messengers providing insights into the most energetic cosmic processes; detecting them efficiently requires improved methods that overcome limitations of traditional particle detectors, especially for highly inclined air showers.
AI.method: A reconstruction algorithm based on the maximum radio emission depth ($X^{\text{radio}}_{\text{max}}$) was developed to distinguish deeply developing neutrino-induced air showers from cosmic ray backgrounds, using ground-based radio antennas and simulations of electron neutrino charged-current-induced air showers.
AI.result: The method shows improved trigger efficiency, reconstruction performance, effective area, and aperture for a reference antenna array, significantly enhancing sensitivity to very inclined showers above 1 EeV, complementing traditional detection techniques and proving applicable to future radio observatories like GRAND.
AI.conclusion: Radio detection using the proposed reconstruction algorithm effectively identifies UHE neutrinos by exploiting their unique shower development signatures, offering a scalable approach that enhances sensitivity and paves the way for future observations of these high-energy cosmic messengers.

title: On the redshift evolution of the spin parameter in cosmological simulations
comment: 13 pages, accepted for publication in PASA
summary: Although the spin parameter of dark matter halos is well known to follow a log-normal distribution at fixed epoch, its quantitative redshift evolution - encompassing both the mean and the dispersion - remains only partially explored. Prior studies either lack the mass resolution required to establish reliable evolutionary trends or do not provide analytical relations that enable forward modelling. Using a suite of LCDM N-body simulations with controlled resolution across the redshift range 0 < z < 5, we characterise the evolution of the mean and dispersion of the Peebles (lambda) and Bullock (lambda') definitions of spin. We find a mild but statistically robust linear evolution for ln(lambda) and a non-monotonic trend with a turnover at z ~ 1 - 2 for ln lambda', which we verify are unaffected by mass resolution of choice of halo definition. We provide closed-form fitting functions for these trends that allow modellers to draw physically motivated spin values at any redshift within our range of validity. This is a practical, redshift-dependent alternative to the common assumption of a constant spin distribution, and provides a useful input to semi-empirical and semi-analytic models of galaxy formation.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the redshift evolution of dark matter halo spin parameters using high-resolution N-body simulations, finding evolving trends in spin distributions and delivering fitting functions for galaxy formation modeling.
AI.motivation: To quantitatively characterize the redshift evolution of the spin parameter distribution of dark matter halos, including both its mean and dispersion, which remains partially unexplored with reliable trends and analytical relations.
AI.method: Used a suite of LCDM N-body simulations with controlled mass resolution spanning redshifts 0 < z < 5 to measure the evolution of mean and dispersion for Peebles (lambda) and Bullock (lambda') spin definitions, verifying effects of mass resolution and halo definition choice.
AI.result: Found a mild but statistically robust linear evolution of ln(lambda) and a non-monotonic trend with turnover at z~1-2 for ln(lambda'), unaffected by resolution or halo definition; provided closed-form fitting functions for redshift-dependent spin evolution.
AI.conclusion: The study provides practical, physically motivated, redshift-dependent fitting functions for dark matter halo spin parameters that improve upon the common assumption of constant spin distribution, enabling better semi-empirical and semi-analytic galaxy formation models.

title: Signature of iron line profile from a Kerr-like wormhole
summary: Broad, skewed iron K$α$ emission lines in the X-ray spectra of accreting black holes encode key information about the spacetime geometry of the innermost disk. While the Kerr metric is standard for spin measurements, horizonless alternatives like traversable "Kerr-like" wormholes can mimic many black hole signatures, challenging current data interpretations. We develop a relativistic reflection framework incorporating Kerr-like wormhole geometries to predict iron line distortions and assess the feasibility of distinguishing event horizons from wormhole throats.Using a custom ray-tracing subroutine, we implement two \textsc{XSPEC} modules: \texttt{kwline} for $δ$-function profiles and \texttt{kwconv} for full reflection spectra, parameterized by spin, throat radius, and shape-function coefficients. We compute a dense grid of line profiles and generate synthetic \textit{NuSTAR} spectra with realistic response matrices. By fitting these simulations with canonical Kerr models, we quantify deviations attributable to wormhole geometries.We find that Kerr-like wormholes produce narrower Fe K$α$ lines with suppressed red wings as the throat parameter $λ$ increases. In 50 ks \textit{NuSTAR} simulations ($λ=0.9, a_*=0.998$), simple convolutional models (\texttt{kerrconv}) can mimic the wormhole spectrum. However, self-consistent models like \texttt{relxillCp} result in statistical failure, yielding structured residuals and unphysical parameter pegging (e.g., emissivity $q_{\rm in} \to 10$). We conclude that large-throat wormholes are detectable in high-quality X-ray spectra if analyzed with fully consistent reflection models rather than post-processing approximations.

AI.tldr: This study introduces a modeling framework to assess how Kerr-like wormholes distort iron Kα emission lines in X-ray spectra, demonstrating that while simple models can mimic wormhole signatures, fully consistent reflection models reveal detectable spectral differences, enabling observational distinction between black holes and wormholes.
AI.motivation: To differentiate black hole event horizons from traversable Kerr-like wormholes by analyzing iron Kα emission line distortions in X-ray spectra, which challenge current interpretations that assume Kerr metrics.
AI.method: Development of a relativistic reflection framework integrating Kerr-like wormhole geometries, implemented via custom ray-tracing subroutines and two XSPEC modules (kwline for δ-function profiles and kwconv for full reflection spectra); generation of synthetic NuSTAR spectra using realistic response matrices and fitting with canonical Kerr models to quantify deviations due to wormholes.
AI.result: Kerr-like wormholes yield narrower iron Kα lines with diminished red wings as throat parameter λ increases; simple Kerr convolution models can mimic wormhole spectra but fully self-consistent reflection models fail statistically, producing residuals and unphysical parameter values, indicating detectability of large-throat wormholes in high-quality X-ray spectra with appropriate modeling.
AI.conclusion: Large-throat Kerr-like wormholes can be distinguished from black holes in high-quality X-ray observations if fully self-consistent reflection models are employed, as simplistic post-processing models fail to capture key spectral deviations induced by wormhole geometries.

title: How lonely are the Binary Compact Objects Detected by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Collaboration?
summary: Gravitational-wave (GW) observations of compact binary coalescences (CBCs) are traditionally interpreted under the assumption that the binary evolves in isolation. However, in realistic astrophysical environments, brief three-body encounters may perturb the binary's orbital evolution and imprint deviations on the emitted GWs. We develop a physically motivated model for such interactions, retaining Newtonian three-body dynamics supplemented by leading-order ($2.5$PN) radiation-reaction within the binary. We show that such encounters produce a distinctive morphology of dephasing and amplitude modulation in GWs. We search for this kind of distortion from the LIGO--Virgo--KAGRA (LVK) GW catalog GWTC-4 on three events: GW170817, GW190814, and GW230627\_015337, chosen based on high SNR and in-band duration $\gtrsim 10~\mathrm{s}$. We find no statistically significant deviation in the data, which translates into constraints on the absence of any intermediate-mass black hole in the mass range above $\sim 10^2$ M$_\odot$ in the vicinity of these binaries of radius approximately $10^{-1}~\mathrm{AU}$. This arises from robust exclusions arising from fly-by interactions that would dynamically disrupt the binary and are directly ruled out independent of waveform modelling, placing the first upper bound on intermediate-mass black holes near these GW events. In future, with the availability of long-duration GW signals, this new avenue can probe encounters of the binary GW sources with compact objects of lighter masses at distances farther away than 1 AU and hence opens a new window to probe the population of individual compact objects of both astrophysical and primordial origin in astrophysical systems of dense environments ranging from galactic centers to dense globular clusters.

AI.tldr: This paper models how brief three-body encounters affect gravitational-wave signals from binary coalescences and searches for such effects in high-quality LVK data. Finding no deviations, it constrains nearby intermediate-mass black holes and highlights future prospects to probe compact-object populations in dense environments through GW observations.
AI.motivation: Traditional gravitational-wave analyses assume binary evolution in isolation, ignoring possible perturbations from three-body interactions common in realistic dense astrophysical environments.
AI.method: Developed a physically motivated model incorporating Newtonian three-body dynamics and leading-order (2.5PN) radiation reaction to simulate effects of brief three-body encounters on binary orbital evolution and gravitational waveforms; analyzed data from select high-SNR, long-duration GW events (GW170817, GW190814, GW230627_015337) from the LVK catalog to search for waveform distortions.
AI.result: No statistically significant deviations from isolated binary evolution were found, allowing constraints on the absence of intermediate-mass black holes (>~10^2 M⊙) within ~0.1 AU from these binaries. Dynamical disruptions due to fly-by interactions are ruled out, placing the first upper bounds on such black holes near these GW events.
AI.conclusion: Short three-body encounters can imprint measurable modulations on GW signals, but current observations show no evidence for such interactions near analyzed binaries, thereby constraining the local population of intermediate-mass black holes. Future long-duration GW detections will improve sensitivity, offering a novel probe of compact object populations in dense astrophysical environments ranging from galactic centers to globular clusters.

title: Synchrotron polarization of anisotropic electron distribution in GRB prompt emission
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, 1 table. Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: In gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), the electron pitch angle ($α$) is usually assumed to be isotropically distributed. However, recent numerical simulations indicate that only the high-energy electrons (with Lorentz factors $γ>γ_{iso}$) are distributed isotropically, whereas the low-energy electrons (with $γ<γ_{iso}$) follow an energy-dependent anisotropic distribution during magnetic reconnection. The mean value of $\sin^2 α$ approximately follows the relation $\langle \sin^2 α\rangle \propto γ^{m}$ for $γ<γ_{iso}$. In principle, polarization measurements may help us constrain the pitch-angle distribution of electrons in GRBs, since different pitch-angle distributions produce distinct synchrotron polarization signatures. The polarization of GRBs produced by isotropically distributed electrons has been extensively studied. In this paper, we investigate synchrotron polarization produced by anisotropically distributed electrons within a globally toroidal magnetic field in GRB prompt emission. Our results show that the synchrotron PDs in the $γ$-ray and X-ray bands produced by anisotropically distributed electrons are systematically lower than those produced by isotropically distributed electrons, while the PD in the optical band could be either lower or higher than that of isotropically distributed electrons, depending primarily on the value of the energy slope $m$. In addition, we compared our numerical results with observational data, and the comparison suggests that an anisotropic distribution of electrons may offer a potential explanation for the PD and spectral data of some GRBs.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how anisotropic electron pitch angle distributions affect synchrotron polarization in GRB prompt emission, finding systematic reductions in gamma-ray and X-ray polarization degrees and variable optical polarization, with implications for interpreting observational data.
AI.motivation: Recent numerical simulations suggest that electron pitch angle distributions in GRBs are anisotropic for low-energy electrons, challenging the common assumption of isotropy and motivating investigation into how this affects synchrotron polarization.
AI.method: The study analyzes synchrotron polarization signatures by modeling anisotropic electron pitch angle distributions within a globally toroidal magnetic field in GRB prompt emission, focusing on energy-dependent electron anisotropy characterized by a power-law relation in pitch angle distribution.
AI.result: The synchrotron polarization degrees (PDs) in gamma-ray and X-ray bands from anisotropically distributed electrons are systematically lower than those from isotropic distributions, while optical band PDs can be either lower or higher depending on the energy slope parameter; comparison with observational data suggests anisotropic electron distributions can explain polarization and spectral features in some GRBs.
AI.conclusion: Electron pitch angle anisotropy significantly influences synchrotron polarization in GRB prompt emission, offering a viable explanation for observed polarization degrees and spectral properties not accounted for by isotropic models.

title: Ultra-high-energy $γ$-ray imprints from PeV particles accelerated by supernova remnants
summary: The quest for the origin of cosmic ray (CRs) is a fundamental issue in astrophysics. Shocks of supernova remnants (SNRs) have been considered as the dominant contributors to Galactic CRs below the spectral knee near $\sim 3$ petaelectronvolt (PeV). Whether SNRs are efficient accelerators of particles beyond PeV energies has long been debated. Here we report observations of very-high-energy $γ$-ray emission up to hundreds of TeV from two middle age shell-type SNRs, G150.3$+$4.5 and $γ$-Cygni, with the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO). Two (or three) distinct morphological/spectral components with convex spectral shapes are observed in both sources, with the low-energy one being more extended than the high-energy one. %Although it is possible that these high-energy components may be driven by powerful pulsars, The likely association of the high-energy component with molecular clouds at similar distances, and the weakness/absence of pulsar wind nebulae (PWNe) inside these SNRs clearly indicate for the first time that the highest energy emission is produced by collision of hadronic CRs up to PeV energies with the clouds. These results are compatible with the classic model prediction that PeV particles accelerated near the end of the free expansion phase of SNR evolution can illuminate nearby molecular clouds (MCs) to produce strong $γ$-ray emission.

AI.tldr: This paper reports LHAASO observations of very-high-energy gamma rays from two middle-aged supernova remnants, revealing that hadronic cosmic rays accelerated up to PeV energies collide with nearby molecular clouds to produce gamma-ray emission, supporting SNRs as sources of Galactic cosmic rays up to PeV energies.
AI.motivation: To address the fundamental astrophysical question of the origin of cosmic rays and determine whether supernova remnants can accelerate particles beyond PeV energies.
AI.method: Observations of very-high-energy gamma-ray emission up to hundreds of TeV from two middle-age shell-type supernova remnants, G150.3+4.5 and gamma-Cygni, using the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO). Detailed morphological and spectral analyses were performed to identify distinct emission components and their associations.
AI.result: Identification of two or three distinct morphological and spectral components with convex spectral shapes in both SNRs. The high-energy emission components are likely produced by hadronic cosmic rays up to PeV energies interacting with nearby molecular clouds, with little contribution from pulsar wind nebulae. These observations support the classic model that PeV particles accelerated near the end of the free expansion phase of SNRs illuminate molecular clouds to produce strong gamma-ray emission.
AI.conclusion: The study provides strong evidence that middle-age shell-type SNRs can accelerate hadronic cosmic rays up to PeV energies and that these particles produce very-high-energy gamma-ray emission by interacting with nearby molecular clouds, confirming supernova remnants as plausible sources of Galactic PeV cosmic rays.

title: Radiative feedbacks as drivers for quasi-periodic-oscillation activity in black-hole X-ray binaries
comment: 20 pages, 22 figures, 11 tables, accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Black-hole X-ray binaries (BHXRBs) in the hard and hard-intermediate spectral states commonly exhibit prominent type-C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in their X-ray power spectra. Despite extensive observational and theoretical efforts, the physical mechanism responsible for these oscillations has not yet been firmly established. The disk-corona system in BHXRBs is radiatively coupled, as hard X-ray emission from the corona can be reprocessed by the accretion disk and re-emitted as soft photons that contribute to cooling the coronal electrons. Aim of the present study is to examine whether this feedback can give rise to limit cycles having the spectro-temporal properties of QPOs. We model the coronal emission using a one-zone radiation framework and solve the time-dependent kinetic equations for electrons and photons. Electrons are energized by some unspecified process and cool via inverse Compton scattering of soft photons originating from (i) the accretion disk and (ii) disk reprocessing of the hard radiation produced in the corona. When electron cooling is dominated by soft photons reprocessed in the accretion disk, the disk-corona system undergoes limit-cycle oscillations. For a subset of the model parameters, these oscillations reproduce key properties of type-C QPOs observed in BHXRBs. The oscillation frequency depends on the coronal radius and on the energization timescale, while the resulting X-ray spectra are well described by power laws extending up to energies of ~ 10-100 keV. These calculations confirm and extend earlier semi-analytical results obtained with simplified treatments. Owing to the scale-invariant nature of the model, the results can be readily extrapolated to other accreting systems, such as Active Galactic Nuclei.

AI.tldr: This study uses a radiation model of the disk-corona system in black-hole X-ray binaries to show that radiative feedback can induce oscillations matching type-C QPOs, explaining their origin and linking oscillation properties to physical parameters.
AI.motivation: To investigate the physical mechanism behind type-C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) seen in the X-ray power spectra of black-hole X-ray binaries (BHXRBs), focusing on the radiative coupling between the accretion disk and corona.
AI.method: Modeled the coronal emission using a one-zone radiation framework and solved time-dependent kinetic equations for electrons and photons, incorporating electron energization and cooling via inverse Compton scattering of soft photons from the accretion disk and its reprocessed radiation.
AI.result: Found that when electron cooling is dominated by reprocessed soft photons from the disk, the disk-corona system exhibits limit-cycle oscillations reproducing key properties of type-C QPOs, with oscillation frequency dependent on coronal radius and energization timescale; X-ray spectra match observed power laws up to ~10-100 keV.
AI.conclusion: The radiative feedback between the disk and corona can drive limit-cycle oscillations that account for type-C QPOs in BHXRBs, confirming and extending previous semi-analytical models; this scale-invariant model can be applied to other accreting systems like Active Galactic Nuclei.

title: Exploring the diversity of kilonovae with 3D radiative transfer I. The polar direction
summary: We present 3D kilonova radiative transfer simulations for a series of binary neutron star merger models. The masses of the neutron stars are varied as well as the total mass of the system and two different equations of state were used (SFHO and DD2), producing a range in dynamical ejecta masses and elemental abundance patterns. In this paper, we focus on the bolometric light curves and spectra in the polar direction for comparison with observations of the kilonova AT2017gfo. We calculate line-by-line opacities and include new calibrated lanthanide atomic data. All of the simulated spectra show strong features from Sr II, La III, Gd III and Ce III, which appear to correspond to features identified in AT2017gfo, although the simulated features are generally more blueshifted. The models with the lowest lanthanide fraction in the polar direction also show a Y II feature. Ce III, Ce II, Nd III and Nd II play an important role in shaping the spectral continuum. While the bolometric luminosities in the polar direction vary with the ejecta mass of each model, we find only little sensitivity of the spectral properties to the merger configuration. Our study demonstrates that dynamical ejecta alone can reproduce (although at earlier times) many spectral properties of AT2017gfo, suggesting dynamical ejecta may have a strong impact on the early spectral evolution. However, future simulations are needed to also elucidate the role of other ejecta components for shaping the kilonova spectrum.

AI.tldr: 3D simulations of neutron star merger kilonovae show that dynamical ejecta can explain many early spectral features of AT2017gfo, highlighting their importance in shaping early kilonova spectra.
AI.motivation: To understand the spectral and light curve properties of kilonovae resulting from binary neutron star mergers and compare these with observations of AT2017gfo, focusing on the role of dynamical ejecta.
AI.method: 3D radiative transfer simulations of kilonovae from binary neutron star mergers with varied neutron star masses, total system masses, and two different equations of state (SFHO and DD2). Simulations include line-by-line opacities and new calibrated lanthanide atomic data, analyzing bolometric light curves and spectra in the polar direction.
AI.result: Simulated spectra display strong features from Sr II, La III, Gd III, Ce III, consistent with features in AT2017gfo but generally more blueshifted. Models with low lanthanide fraction show Y II features. Ce III, Ce II, Nd III, and Nd II influence spectral continuum formation. Bolometric luminosities vary with ejecta mass but spectral properties are weakly sensitive to merger configurations. Dynamical ejecta alone can reproduce many early spectral properties of AT2017gfo.
AI.conclusion: Dynamical ejecta from neutron star mergers significantly impact early kilonova spectral evolution and can largely account for observed features in AT2017gfo, though additional ejecta components must be considered in future simulations for a comprehensive understanding.

title: Dense Matter and Compact Stars in Strong Magnetic Fields
comment: Invited review article for publication in "Universe"
summary: Compact stars serve as natural systems where matter exists at densities far beyond those achievable in laboratory experiments. Among them, magnetars are expected to possess interior magnetic fields that may reach values of the order of $10^{17}-10^{18}$ G. These extreme conditions are expected to alter the microscopic and macroscopic properties of dense matter. In this review, we examine how strong magnetic fields affect fermionic matter through mechanisms such as Landau quantization and anomalous magnetic moment interactions. We further discuss the behaviour of magnetized hadronic matter within relativistic mean-field approaches and consider the possible emergence of additional degrees of freedom, including hyperons, $Δ$ resonances, meson condensates and quark matter. The consequences of these effects for neutron-star structure and observational constraints are also briefly outlined.

AI.tldr: This review examines how ultra-strong magnetic fields in magnetars modify dense matter properties, exploring theoretical effects on particle interactions and neutron star structure.
AI.motivation: To understand how extreme magnetic fields inside magnetars influence dense matter properties beyond laboratory-accessible densities.
AI.method: Review of theoretical mechanisms affecting fermionic matter under strong magnetic fields, including Landau quantization and magnetic moment interactions; use of relativistic mean-field models to study magnetized hadronic matter; consideration of additional particle species and phases.
AI.result: Identification of significant modifications in dense matter properties due to strong magnetic fields, influencing particle compositions and neutron star structure.
AI.conclusion: Strong magnetic fields in magnetars substantially alter microscopic and macroscopic properties of dense matter, affecting neutron star structure and potentially observable features.
